newsitem.title: USA: Clinton marks inaugural with plea for civility.
newsitem.headline: Clinton marks inaugural with plea for civility.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Monday savored a moment no Democrat since Franklin Roosevelt has enjoyed as he celebrated his second inaugural and talked of leading a more civil U.S. society into the 21st Century.

Clinton, whose first term was marred by fierce bickering with congressional Republicans and numerous probes into his public and private behaviour, was to deliver his inaugural address at the U.S. Capitol after being sworn in for another four years by Supreme Court Chief Justice William Rehnquist at noon EST (1700 GMT).

Before the ceremony, Clinton and his family and Vice President Al Gore and his family attended a prayer service at the Metropolitan AME Church, a predominantly black church in the centre of Washington.

Black political leader Jesse Jackson, an ordained minister and candidate for the Democratic presidential nomination in 1988, spoke at the service and asked for a moment of silence for the son of popular comedian Bill Cosby, who was murdered in Los Angeles last week.
It was the first official event on an inaugural schedule that drew thousands of loyal Democrats and ordinary citizens to Washington for festivities that were to go on until early Tuesday morning.
The inauguration coincided with a federal holiday honouring Martin Luther King, Jr., the assassinated civil rights leader, a day traditionally devoted to reflections on racial harmony.
After the service the Clintons and Gores were to return to the White House for a coffee with congressional leaders.
In a bylined article in Monday's Washington Times, Clinton said the United States faced immense challenges, and that his goal was "to prepare the nation for the new century."
"My one great hope is that we will accomplish our journey in the right spirit, with civility, respect and all our citizens feeling that they are part of our national community," he wrote.

Rather than just bask in the glory of being the first Democratic president to be re-elected to a second term since 1936, Clinton seemed eager to make his inaugural speech a serious appeal for both political and racial healing.

"I hope that I can set a tone on Monday and in the days ahead that will help flush the poison out of the atmosphere and get people to thinking about the folks that sent us here," he told the Washington Post in an interview on Sunday.

The inaugural marked the crowning moment of a remarkable comeback by Clinton, who was all but written off politically after voters repudiated his Democratic Party in the 1994 mid-term elections and gave Republicans control of Congress for the first time in 40 years.

Clinton bounced back by moving to the centre politically and outflanking Republicans in a bitter budget battle that shut down the government twice in late 1995 and early 1996. He cemented his remarkable rebound by defeating Republican rival Bob Dole in last November's presidential election.
At the same time however, the voters left Congress in Republican hands, which will mean continued divided government for at least half of Clinton's second term.

As Clinton revelled in inaugural pageantry, a New York Times/CBS poll published on Monday showed the 50-year-old Arkansan entering his second term with a 60 percent approval rating and with two-thirds of the country saying they were optimistic that his second term would be a success.
In a brief interview on NBC's "Today Show," Clinton said the election result showed the American people "want the Congress and me to work together. They want us to lay down our partisan sniping."
"We have to think big thoughts," he said.
Clinton has stressed that his top second-term priority is an agreement to balance the federal budget.

Over the weekend he said he hoped this would pave the way for refinancing Social Security and Medicare, the federal pensions system and the health service for the elderly and disabled. They are the most complicated domestic issues he faces.
Under fire for the Democratic Party's questionable 1996 political financing tactics, he also promised to lead a bipartisan drive to clean up the way campaign money is raised.

"We must work to renew our democracy and restore the American people's confidence in their government. That means first and foremost campaign finance reform," he said in his Washington Times article. Clinton has also promised major efforts to improve U.S. education and protect the environment.
